distillation_scope.manifold_definition: Pulmonary infection and inflammatory lung injury after aspiration of colonized oropharyngeal secretions, gastric contents, or particulate material into the lower respiratory tract. The first-layer leaf is not split by community versus hospital setting, anaerobic burden, stroke, nursing-home residence, or severity.
distillation_scope.subtype_policy: Aspiration triggers, swallowing impairment, impaired consciousness, dental/oral status, care setting, and likely pathogen mix are represented as risk/context and treatment modifiers rather than qualifiers in the disease name.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Macroaspiration or repeated microaspiration delivers colonized oral secretions, gastric fluid, food particles, or sputum into bronchi and dependent alveoli.
Acid, bile, enzymes, and particulate food injure airway epithelium, obstruct bronchi, provoke bronchospasm, atelectasis, and acute neutrophil recruitment before bacterial growth is fully established.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Polymicrobial oral or gastric pathogen burden
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Mixed aerobic, facultative, and anaerobic organisms from the oropharynx or stomach proliferate in injured dependent lung. Modern aspiration pneumonia is often aerobic gram-negative or streptococcal, with anaerobic dominance mainly in poor dentition, necrosis, abscess, or empyema contexts.
Alveolar neutrophil influx, edema, fibrin, and cellular debris fill airspaces, producing crackles, cough, sputum, fever, elevated CRP, and radiographic infiltrate or consolidation.

Aspirated material preferentially injures dependent segments: posterior upper lobes and superior lower lobes when supine, basal lower lobes when upright; chronic silent aspiration can produce recurrent lower/posterior infiltrates and tree-in-bud bronchiolitis.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Shunt physiology and hypoxemic respiratory failure
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Dependent consolidation, atelectasis, bronchial obstruction, and inflammatory edema produce V/Q mismatch and true shunt with tachypnea, dyspnea, low SpO2, low PaO2/FiO2, and possible ventilatory failure.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Systemic inflammatory response and sepsis pressure
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Pulmonary infection can spill into systemic cytokine activity, bacteremia, hypotension, lactate rise, AKI, thrombocytopenia, and delirium, especially in frail elderly or delayed-treatment cases.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Pleural, abscess, and necrotizing complication pressure
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Persistent polymicrobial burden, poor oral anaerobic load, delayed therapy, or obstruction can progress to lung abscess, necrotizing pneumonia, complicated parapneumonic effusion, or empyema.

Dysphagia, impaired cough, vocal-cord dysfunction, altered consciousness, reflux, tube feeding, or poor oral care sustain recurrence risk and weaken treatment response unless aspiration prevention is addressed.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Airway-protection failure increases macroaspiration and repeated microaspiration events.
Aspirated gastric contents or food particles directly injure and obstruct airway surfaces.
The same aspirated material introduces viable oral and gastric flora into injured dependent lung.
Bacterial growth and PAMPs amplify neutrophilic alveolar exudation.
Chemical pneumonitis and obstruction initiate sterile neutrophilic lung injury that can become infected.
Repeated dependent deposition sustains or recurs alveolitis in dependent regions.
Airspace filling and atelectasis create shunt physiology and increased work of breathing.
Higher bacterial burden increases systemic inflammatory and bacteremic risk.
Persistent bacterial burden, especially anaerobic or obstructed infection, can produce abscess or empyema.
Witnessed choking, vomiting, regurgitation, or airway contamination is the observed macroaspiration counterpart.
Silent aspiration presents as recurrent pneumonias or chronic cough without obvious choking.
Oropharyngeal dysphagia is a major airway-protection substrate for aspiration.
Altered mentation, weak cough, vocal-cord dysfunction, or sedation lowers airway protection.
Vomiting or regurgitation is a common proximate macroaspiration event.
CT, bronchoscopy, or suctioning may reveal sputum, bile, food particles, or secretions in the airway.
Gravity-dependent distribution is a characteristic imaging clue for aspiration.
Recurrent aspiration can produce bronchiolar tree-in-bud or branching centrilobular opacities.
Particulate obstruction and splinting can collapse dependent lung segments.
Alveolar exudate and edema produce radiographic infiltrates.
Airspace filling can appear as consolidation, especially in dependent lobes.
Parapneumonic pleural reaction may accompany aspiration pneumonia.
Airway and alveolar inflammation commonly cause cough, although cough may be absent in frail or neurologically impaired patients.
Neutrophilic airway infection can produce purulent sputum.
Dependent alveolar fluid and consolidation produce crackles or coarse breath sounds.
Lower-lobe or diaphragmatic pleural irritation can rarely present with persistent hiccups.
IL-1, TNF, and IL-6 drive fever; elderly or frail patients may be afebrile.
Fever, hypoxemia, and systemic inflammation raise heart rate.
Tachypnea is an early response to hypoxemia and increased work of breathing.
Gas exchange impairment and work of breathing produce dyspnea unless neurologic blunting masks symptoms.
V/Q mismatch and shunt lower SpO2.
Escalating oxygen or ventilatory support reflects respiratory severity.
PaO2/FiO2 captures severity of oxygen transfer failure.
Severe fatigue, obstruction, or COPD overlap can produce hypercapnia.
Hypercapnic or lactic acidosis can lower arterial pH.
Bacterial pneumonia and stress usually produce leukocytosis, though elderly or marrow-suppressed patients can remain normal.
Neutrophil predominance is common in bacterial aspiration pneumonia.
IL-6-driven acute-phase response raises CRP.
Procalcitonin rises with bacterial infection and sepsis pressure but may be modest in localized aspiration.
Sepsis physiology and dehydration can lower MAP in severe cases.
Shock and severe hypoxemia can elevate lactate.
Sepsis, dehydration, nephrotoxic exposure, or hypoxemia may produce AKI.
Severe infection can consume platelets or suppress marrow response.
Worsening hypoxemia increases near-term respiratory failure risk.
Large-volume aspiration and severe pneumonia can evolve into diffuse alveolar damage.
Persistent hypoxemia, hypercapnia, or airway contamination increases intubation risk.
Sepsis and hypoperfusion raise AKI event risk.
Aspiration pneumonia can produce septic shock in severe or frail cases.
Necrotizing anaerobic or mixed infection can cavitate into lung abscess.
Pleural bacterial extension can create complicated effusion or empyema.
Sepsis physiology is a major near-term mortality pathway.
Respiratory failure is the main proximal fatal pathway.
Abscess, necrosis, and empyema prolong infection and raise death risk.

axes.axis_name: Witnessed aspiration or choking event activity
axes.clinical_interpretation: Observed choking, coughing with meals, regurgitation, vomiting, or airway contamination around symptom onset.
Recurrent pneumonia, chronic cough, or swallow-study evidence of silent aspiration.
Swallowing impairment is a major aspiration substrate but may be absent in single emesis-related aspiration.
Reduced consciousness, weak cough, vocal-cord dysfunction, neurologic disease, sedation, or seizure-related airway risk.
Vomiting or regurgitation can be the proximate aspiration event.
Sputum, bile, food particles, or secretions seen in trachea/bronchi by CT, bronchoscopy, or suctioning.

axes.axis_name: New pulmonary infiltrate or consolidation extent
axes.clinical_interpretation: Generic pneumonia infiltrate axis reused for aspiration-related airspace disease.
Posterior or basal lower-lobe predominance, or dependent upper-lobe/posterior segment involvement in supine patients.
Airspace consolidation from dependent neutrophilic exudate.
Bronchiolar branching/centrilobular opacities are especially relevant to recurrent microaspiration.
Airway obstruction, mucus plugging, splinting, and postoperative physiology can produce atelectasis alongside aspiration pneumonia.
Parapneumonic effusion can accompany aspiration pneumonia but is not required.
Cough may be productive, weak, absent, or blunted depending on airway-protection status.
Copious or purulent sputum supports airway bacterial burden but can be absent.

axes.axis_name: Crackles or coarse breath sounds activity
axes.clinical_interpretation: Coarse crackles or decreased dependent breath sounds reflect airspace disease.
Persistent hiccups are uncommon but can occur with lower-lobe pneumonia or diaphragmatic irritation.
Dyspnea tracks respiratory involvement but may be underreported in frail or neurologically impaired patients.
Fever is common but elderly aspiration pneumonia can present with low-grade fever or no fever.
Reported fever may be more informative than a single afebrile measurement.
Tachypnea is a sensitive sign of pneumonia severity and hypoxemia.
Tachycardia reflects fever, hypoxemia, dehydration, or sepsis.
Hypotension appears in severe sepsis, dehydration, or sedation overlap; many cases remain normotensive.
MAP falls with severe sepsis or shock but can be normal in mild aspiration pneumonia.
SpO2 may be preserved in mild lower-lobe disease but drops sharply with large-volume aspiration or COPD overlap.

axes.axis_name: Oxygen or ventilatory support requirement level
axes.clinical_interpretation: 0 none, 1 low-flow oxygen, 2 high-flow or mask, 3 noninvasive ventilation, 4 invasive ventilation, 5 rescue ventilation/ECMO-level support.
Gas-exchange severity marker; values below 300 indicate clinically important oxygenation impairment.
Absolute PaO2 depends on FiO2 and should be interpreted with oxygen delivery context.
Low or normal in pure tachypnea; high in COPD overlap, fatigue, or ventilatory failure.
Acidemia reflects severe hypercapnia, lactic acidosis, or mixed respiratory/metabolic failure.
Leukocytosis is common; normal WBC does not exclude aspiration pneumonia in elderly or frail patients.
Neutrophil-predominant inflammation supports bacterial lung infection.
CRP tracks inflammatory burden and usually falls after effective therapy.
Higher with bacterial sepsis; may be low in localized or chemical-predominant aspiration.
Anemia is a severity and frailty context rather than defining aspiration pneumonia.
Can be normal, reactive-high, or low with severe sepsis.
Low albumin reflects frailty, inflammation, and mortality risk but is not specific.
Lactate rises in shock, severe work of breathing, or hypoxemia.
AKI is a complication or background context, not a defining axis.
BUN can rise with dehydration, catabolism, AKI, or gastrointestinal bleeding.
Bicarbonate can fall with lactic acidosis or remain normal in isolated pneumonia.
Composite bedside expression of hypoxemia, hypercapnia, respiratory distress, and need for ventilatory support.
Event risk for clinically important acute respiratory failure.
Large-volume aspiration or severe bilateral pneumonia can lead to ARDS.

axes.axis_name: Need for invasive mechanical ventilation hazard
axes.clinical_interpretation: Invasive ventilation risk rises with refractory hypoxemia, hypercapnia, airway contamination, or depressed mental status.
AKI risk tracks sepsis severity, dehydration, and nephrotoxic treatment context.
Shock hazard increases in severe aspiration pneumonia or frail elderly patients.
Anaerobic, necrotizing, or obstructed aspiration infection can evolve into abscess.
Complicated parapneumonic effusion or empyema risk.
Probability that the chosen regimen covers the current bacterial burden.
Treatment context axis for anaerobic activity when abscess, necrosis, empyema, severe periodontal disease, or witnessed gastric aspiration raises anaerobic value.
Adequacy of NPO decisions, swallow assessment, diet texture, feeding position, oral care, tube strategy, and medication/sedation review.
Need for protected airway, suctioning, airway clearance, or enteral feeding precautions.
Vomiting, ileus, shock, or NPO status lowers reliability of oral antibiotics.
Renal dosing and nephrotoxicity context for beta-lactams and adjunctive agents.
Lifespan outcome hazard driven by respiratory failure, sepsis/shock, frailty, recurrent aspiration, abscess/empyema, and delayed active therapy.

axis_couplings.rationale: Witnessed aspiration and visible airway material often occur together but either can be absent.
Dependent extent is a satellite of the overall infiltrate burden.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Stronger when consolidation is bilateral, large-volume, or accompanied by atelectasis/COPD.
axis_couplings.rationale: More airspace disease worsens gas exchange.
Both axes measure oxygenation severity when FiO2 context is available.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Most relevant with bilateral infiltrates or large-volume aspiration.
axis_couplings.rationale: Low PaO2/FiO2 is the primary gas-exchange signal for ARDS-level severity.
Escalating oxygen support predicts intubation risk.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Hypercapnia from COPD overlap, fatigue, or airway obstruction.

axis_couplings.rationale: CRP and leukocytosis are co-driven by systemic inflammation but are not causally upstream of one another.
Respiratory failure is a proximal death pathway.
Septic shock or peri-aspiration circulatory collapse increases near-term death risk.
AKI reflects multiorgan dysfunction and worsens prognosis.
Abscess prolongs infection and source-control burden.
Empyema adds source-control and sepsis risk.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Benefit depends on coverage of oral streptococci, susceptible gram-negatives, and anaerobic components when present.
Renal dosing required to avoid accumulation.

treatments.context_specific_role: Broad aspiration-pneumonia coverage when oral flora and susceptible hospital/community gram-negative organisms are plausible.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Vomiting, ileus, shock, or NPO status makes oral step-down unreliable.

treatments.context_specific_role: Oral completion or mild stable aspiration pneumonia when absorption and coverage are adequate.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Metronidazole adds anaerobic coverage when abscess, necrosis, severe periodontal disease, or gastric aspiration makes it valuable.

treatments.context_specific_role: Separates gram-negative/streptococcal coverage from anaerobic coverage when a cephalosporin backbone is chosen.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Expected benefit rises when resistant gram-negative or healthcare-associated flora remain covered.
Renal dosing and sodium load matter in CKD or AKI.

side_effects.interpretation: AKI signal especially with vancomycin or severe illness

treatments.context_specific_role: Broader IV option for severe aspiration pneumonia, postoperative/hospital exposure, or pseudomonal risk.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Value rises when prior beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor or ceftriaxone exposure is likely inactive against ESBL/AmpC organisms.
Dose adjustment reduces neurotoxicity and accumulation.

side_effects.interpretation: inactive-coverage pressure falls after active carbapenem therapy

treatments.context_specific_role: Escalation or definitive coverage for ESBL-risk or critically ill aspiration pneumonia when narrower coverage is unreliable.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: These agents are most relevant when anaerobic burden is clinically important.

side_effects.interpretation: C. difficile risk is clinically important with clindamycin

treatments.context_specific_role: Narrow allergy or anaerobic-complication option; expected value depends strongly on pathogen mix and toxicity context.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Large shunt fraction can blunt oxygen response and require escalation.
Noninvasive support may worsen aspiration risk when airway protection is poor.

treatments.context_specific_role: Supports oxygenation while antibiotics, airway clearance, and aspiration prevention act.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Clearance benefit is greatest when particulate, bile, or copious secretions remain in the airway.

treatments.context_specific_role: Clear retained aspirate or mucus plugging when imaging, suction, or bronchoscopy shows airway material.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Swallow evaluation, diet modification, positioning, and oral care matter most when dysphagia is present.
Sedation review, airway protection, and feeding-route decisions reduce repeated aspiration.

treatments.context_specific_role: Prevents recurrence and treatment failure from continued aspiration; includes oral care, upright feeding, swallow evaluation, texture change, NPO when unsafe, medication/sedation review, and reflux management.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Drainage benefit depends on drainable pleural infection or abscess source-control need.

treatments.context_specific_role: Chest tube, image-guided drainage, fibrinolytics, VATS, or abscess drainage when complications become source-control problems.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Hemodynamic support is useful when shock physiology is present.
Over-resuscitation can worsen oxygenation in pneumonia or ARDS.

treatments.context_specific_role: Supportive shock care while active antibiotics and airway/source control take effect.

axis_response_modulation.rationale: Frail elderly patients may have low-grade or absent fever.
Age and frailty strongly worsen aspiration pneumonia prognosis.
Stroke, dementia, Parkinson disease, ALS, or bulbar disease impair swallowing and cough.
Observed dysphagia directly raises aspiration probability.
Loss of airway reflexes around seizures or altered consciousness raises macroaspiration likelihood.
Sedation, opioids, intubation, and postoperative state reduce airway protection.
Postoperative atelectasis can overlap with aspiration injury.
Vomiting/regurgitation immediately before symptoms is a high-value aspiration context.
Tube feeding does not eliminate aspiration and can coexist with reflux and secretion aspiration.
Poor oral source raises anaerobic and mixed-flora burden.
Poor dentition and anaerobic burden increase abscess risk.
Bedbound patients aspirate into posterior dependent segments.
Healthcare exposure increases resistant gram-negative probability.
Reflux, gastric retention, obstruction, or gastroparesis raise regurgitation risk.
Diabetes can impair host defense and gastric motility, but it is a modest nonspecific modifier.

supportive_care: Preserve the first-layer diagnosis as aspiration pneumonia; do not split by CAP/HAP, elderly, stroke, anaerobic, nursing-home, or severe subtype.

Evaluate aspiration risk: witnessed choking/vomiting, dysphagia, cough with meals, impaired consciousness, neurologic disease, sedating medications, reflux, tube feeding, poor oral hygiene, and care setting.
Chest imaging should assess gravity-dependent distribution, lower/posterior predominance, airway material, atelectasis, cavitation, abscess, pleural effusion, and empyema.
Obtain sputum and blood cultures in severe disease or treatment failure, but pathogen identity and susceptibility belong in confirmatory or post-workup context for presentation-only ranking.
Use oxygen escalation according to hypoxemia and work of breathing; protect airway early when consciousness or secretion burden makes noninvasive support unsafe.
Use lung-protective ventilation when invasive ventilation or ARDS physiology occurs.
Airway suctioning and bronchoscopy are most valuable for large-volume particulate aspiration, mucus plugging, or persistent lobar collapse.
Swallow evaluation, NPO decision, diet texture changes, upright feeding, oral care, and sedation/medication review are disease-modifying recurrence controls, not afterthoughts.
De-escalate antibiotics when cultures, clinical course, and setting make narrower coverage safe; avoid unnecessary prolonged anaerobic pressure when abscess/empyema/necrosis risk is low.
Drain empyema, complicated parapneumonic effusion, or selected abscess/source-control lesions when medical therapy alone cannot clear the infection.
Monitor for respiratory failure, ARDS, sepsis/shock, AKI, C. difficile, recurrent aspiration, and post-discharge swallowing/nutrition safety.
quality_notes: No treatment ordering labels are used; treatment choice is left to forward simulation and RMST scoring.
Anaerobic risk is modeled as context and treatment-modifier probability rather than as a disease-name qualifier.

New axes that should receive horizontal review include witnessed_aspiration_event_activity, dependent_pulmonary_infiltrate_extent, aspirated_airway_material_presence, tree_in_bud_opacity_extent, atelectasis_extent, purulent_sputum_activity, crackles_activity, hiccup_activity, anaerobic_coverage_probability, aspiration_prevention_adequacy, lung_abscess_hazard, and empyema_hazard.
